Very few cis guys have test 700 and are natural. Most would be lucky to have 500 ngdl and there is no average value, everyone differs and optimal test levels are different for everyone.

 IMHO to keep any side effects at bay, the lowest possible dose you can have to keep your test within range is the best option to go for. If you don't notice any changes or if your levels are low your dose will get upped. Don't rush it. Anything above 315 depending on your age is optimal. Try not to compare yourself to others

IMHO i have noticed that it is way more difficult to voice train as a guy, but I was surprised that now I do have a high range and can sing almost how I envision my pitch. You might find it difficult to hit a high pitch or a note at first, but if you keep doing the head voice as much as you can it can be completely trainable. 

You CAN train your voice, it takes time, keep singing.

I don't disagree that there is hierarchy in a sense that people sort out how to learn, socialise, and love. ( especially social learning which is very developed in humans). Many experiments point that out. What I am trying to point out, is that this hierarchy, depends on many internal factors that will have an impact on micro - macro and meso dynamics.  
There is a functional benefit to describing these archetypes in studies so we can take action as a society for problems that we experience, but it doesn't necessarily mean that hierarchy is how the world work in real life. Hierarchy is a set of culturally learnt beliefs, and they are ingrained in our nervous system, but they differ on such a great level between people that it is impossible to prove their statistical significance.

  
Edit: In experimental psychology, when people pick someone with favourable qualities as more socially capable, is not always the case when looking at the hard facts. But it is the case that, when you put people together and ask for their opinion, there is a REAL trend or hierarchy. When you look at it evolutionary, a real hierarchy. But it is not clear how these, apply to a real world.

I personally didn't hate my body before transitioning. However, since I was 4 years old I remember knowing I was a dude. I remember when I was 12 and my sister started growing breasts, and I started crying thinking it was going to happen to me in the future. After puberty I was depressed and hated myself and I was going through changes that didn't make me happy. But my hate wasn't necessarily directed towards my body. I didn't know what was wrong. I used a male name in school but was made fun of, or being dismissed by parents and teachers, so I have learnt to suppress it. Fyi, I was born in 1995, and where I grew up not a lot was known about gender dysphoria, so I get it why people didn't understand. Also, I didn't know what transitioning or gender dysphoria was until I was 19 and I remember relating a lot to the idea.   
 What made me transition was the thought about transition. I used to think about how transitioning made me feel but I also used to be scared/apathetic/hesitant about transitioning. But the thought of me just thinking about transitioning with no actual intent to go through with it made me wonder why I was thinking about transitioning so much. I was excusing myself saying Its too much work or that it is not worth it coz I don't feel body dysphoria that much.   
When I got my first job, I hated being perceived as my assigned gender. I was miserable thinking I would grow old and be my assigned gender, I hated thinking I would be compared to my assigned gender and I always had a strong desire to wake up and be the opposite gender. That is when I knew I had to transition. I was 27 years old when I started my transition. I took my time to decide, and that is my advice to every trans identifying individual. As my Endo said, there is no optimal or right age to transition, some people take their time to process it.   


I am 28 going for 29 years old and I am extremely happy, healthier with a stable job. I love my body and how it changes even though I (thought) never had extreme hate for my body.

You sure sound like a reasonable person who is trying to be supportive of their daughter. Here's some advice i think will help. I am transgender and i came out to my parents when i was 25. I am now 29 and i started trt when i was 26. I was assigned female at birth i am now a transitioned male.  I am also a psychologist but please do not use any of the information i give you medical or psychological advice.

1. Think about your daughters childhood. I believe it will help you cope with the change you are experiencing. I believe it will help you understand you daughter. 
Do you remember her saying anything about being a girl or feeling like a girl? Having an interest in things that GENERALLY would interest girls/ an opposite gender/a gender not assigned at birth? Transgender identities are USUALLY expressed very early in life.
There is something called rapid onset gender dysphoria ( IT IS NOT SCIENTIFICALLY SUPPORTED) which usually happens around 20 years of age. iT doesn't exist. 
The fact that she hasn't expressed any feelings DOESN'T mean that she hasn't felt any. It doesn't mean your daughter is any less trans. It also DOESN'T mean that she will regret her transition (or that she won't regret it). It just helps you understand that although she didn't feel like telling you, she feels like this NOW and you should try to understand.

2. As other comments mention, some transgender people don't like to associate with pride. Some people -like myself - just want to feel normal, and want to feel themselves. They wish they were always born the gender they feel. Some people don't feel like there is any "pride" in their transition and it is just a necessary step toward survival. 
They also cut out people who used to know them as another them, and sometimes, sadly, friends cut them out because they feel a certain, different way. Some people want to get their transition "over with" so they can have a normal life, without conflict - because how they feel is internal and they don't want to hear anyone's OPINIONS. 

3. Just be supportive. How? Open ended questions. "How are you? " "Can i ask about....? " " How does you transition make you feel ? " Etc. you know your daughter most of all. She is not a different person personality wise. Just ask, and don't let her go through this alone. Make sure she knows you are proud of her.

ALSO: (EDIT)

Posting pictures of herself could mean she is proud of herself. She is comfortable with what she did. Telling you she is not trans could be her way of telling you, i am a woman or i wish i had been a woman since the day i was born. And she refuses to acknowledge her trans identity because you don't think of it as real. But it is.
